name: Interpolation degree
description: Minimum degree of an interpolating polynomial
definition: The **Interpolation Degree** of $\mathcal{H}$ is the smallest degree needed to interpolate every real-valued function on $\mathcal{H}$. Equivalently, it is the minimum, over bases of $\mathbb{R}[x]/V(\mathcal{H})$, of the largest degree of a basis element.
graph_summary: The least polynomial degree sufficient to interpolate arbitrary functions on the class.
origin_references: Introduced as interpolation degree for Boolean-cube subsets by Moran and Rashtchian in \cite{moran2015shattered}.

monotonic.proof: If degree-$d$ polynomials interpolate every function on $\mathcal H$, their restrictions interpolate every function on a subfamily. Hence passing to a subfamily cannot require a larger degree.

c_monotonic.proof: Restrict an interpolating basis to the conditioned fibre and substitute the fixed coordinates.  This cannot increase the degree needed to interpolate functions on that fibre.

doubly_monotonic.proof: By definition, doubly monotonicity requires both subfamily monotonicity and projection monotonicity; the recorded failure of one of them rules it out.

strictly_monotonic.proof: By definition, strictly monotonicity requires both doubly monotonicity and strict c-monotonicity; the recorded failure of one of them rules it out.

p_monotonic.proof: Counterexample: $\mathcal H=\{001,010,011,100\}$ has interpolation degree 1, since the coordinate functions separate its four points. Projecting away the first coordinate gives the full two-cube, whose interpolation degree is 2.
